title: India 100 GW Nuclear Target Anchors Asia Bid To Dominate Global Atomic Energy Expansion
full_text:
India’s ambition to scale its nuclear power capacity from just 8.8 gigawatts today to 100 gigawatts by 2047 underscores the scale of Asia’s long-term energy transformation.
That target is not an outlier but rather a reflection of a broader regional push that already commands nearly three-quarters of the world’s new nuclear construction activity.
According to Global Energy Monitor data cited by Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire, Asia accounts for 66 gigawatts of the 91 gigawatts of nuclear capacity currently under construction globally.
That 73% share positions the region as the undisputed center of gravity for atomic energy development, dwarfing construction activity in Europe and North America combined.
China is driving the bulk of that momentum, with more than 43 gigawatts of nuclear capacity actively under construction within its borders.
India, Japan, and South Korea collectively contribute roughly 18 gigawatts to the regional total, rounding out a quartet of nations reshaping the global nuclear landscape.
The ambitions extend beyond raw construction numbers, with both Japan and South Korea having stepped back from plans to add new coal-fired generation capacity.
Analysts argue that a sustained build-out of nuclear alongside renewables could meaningfully erode Asia’s long-running dependence on coal and natural gas for power generation.
The region’s coal and gas demand trajectory has long been a dominant factor in global energy markets, and any structural shift away from fossil fuels would carry significant economic consequences worldwide.
India’s target in particular represents one of the most dramatic planned expansions of atomic capacity by any single nation, requiring more than a tenfold increase over roughly two decades.
Whether project timelines, financing, and regulatory frameworks across Asia can keep pace with the stated ambitions will determine how quickly the regional nuclear buildout translates into actual generation capacity.
What the data makes clear is that the next chapter of global nuclear power is being written overwhelmingly in Asia, with China holding the pen for the largest share of that story.
